Discover What You Know
Learning Objectives
Differentiate between the processes involved in innate immunity and adaptive immunity.
Characterize the inflammatory pathways after infection and physical injury.
Identify the mechanisms by which immune cells communicate with the musculoskeletal
system.
Review particle-induced osteolysis as an example of osteoimmunology.
Immunity
Innate Immunity
Innate immunity is the body’s first line of defense against pathogens that breach epithelial
barriers.

Innate immunity is characterized by rapid but nonspecific responses.
Innate immunity typically is induced by the activation of pattern-recognition receptors that
discriminate between groups of pathogens rather than recognize specific pathogens.

Innate Immunity
The primary cell types that contribute to innate immunity are members of the myeloid
lineage, such as macrophages, neutrophils, and dendritic cells.
Initial responses (0 to 4 hours) result from the complement system and resident cells,
primarily macrophages and epithelial cells, that phagocytose pathogens and produce
antimicrobial enzymes, antimicrobial peptides, and pro-inflammatory cytokines. The
cytokines activate the acute-phase response and recruit additional innate immune cells
that are responsible for the second group of responses (4 to 96 hours). During this
phase, neutrophil recruitment typically predominates initially, followed by the
recruitment of macrophages. A third group of responses (>96 hours) are a result of
antigen presentation by dendritic cells and other phagocytes to induce adaptive
immunity.
Pattern-recognition receptors were given this name by Charles Janeway in 1989 to
indicate that each of them is activated by a range of pathogen-derived molecules that
share a conserved structural pattern rather than a specific structure and are detected by
antibodies or classical lock-and-key receptors.1 The primary pattern-recognition receptor
for gram-negative bacteria is toll-like receptor 4 (TLR4). Homodimers of TLR4 are
activated by binding of lipopolysaccharide, a pathogen-associated molecular pattern
(PAMP) produced by gram-negative bacteria. The primary pattern-recognition receptor
for gram-positive bacteria is TLR2. TLR2 is less specific than TLR4 because it
heterodimerizes with TLR1 or TLR6, and those heterodimers are activated by binding of
multiple PAMPs, including lipoteichoic acids from gram-positive bacteria (TLR2/TLR6
heterodimers), diacyl lipopeptides from gram-positive bacteria and mycoplasma
(TLR2/TLR6), and triacyl lipopeptides from gram-negative bacteria and mycoplasma
(TLR2/TLR1). Activation of many TLRs also can be increased by endogenous mammalian
molecules known alternatively as alarmins or damage-associated molecular patterns

that are released by damaged and dying cells. The concept of danger signals released by
cellular damage was originally proposed by Polly Matzinger in 1994.2 Whether alarmins
themselves directly activate the TLRs or whether they facilitate TLR activation via low
levels of PAMPs remains a subject of controversy.3,4 Most of the TLRs are cell surface
receptors; however, TLR3, TLR7, and TLR9 are primarily expressed on intracellular
endosomes where they are activated by bacterial and viral nucleic acids. The TLRs
activate multiple intracellular signaling pathways. The best characterized is the nuclear
factor-κB pathway, which increases transcription of many inflammatory genes, including
interleukin (IL)-1a, IL-1ß, IL-6, and tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-a.
Adaptive Immunity
Adaptive immunity is a response to specific antigens.
Adaptive immunity is primarily attributable to lymphoid cells.
Adaptive immunity is characterized by complex regulatory mechanisms that fine-tune immune
responses.

Adaptive Immunity
Adaptive immunity is induced by dendritic cells and other phagocytes, typically members
of the innate immune system, that present antigen and co-stimulatory molecules to cells
of the adaptive immune system. Presentation of antigen and co-stimulatory molecules to
naïve lymphocytes induces activation and clonal selection of antigen specific cells and
their differentiation into mature effector lymphocytes and memory lymphocytes that
confer immunologic memory by responding to re-exposure to the specific antigen. The
initial response to a new antigen is relatively slow (≥6 days), but the secondary response
by memory lymphocytes is faster (≥1 day) and of much larger magnitude. Those memory
responses account for the success of vaccines.
The primary effector cells that contribute to adaptive immunity are members of the
lymphoid lineage, such as B cells and T cells. B cells contribute by producing antibodies
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Immunology and Inflammation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001002
3/13

specific to individual antigens. CD8-positive T cells primarily contribute by killing
pathogen-infected host cells.
Naïve CD4-positive T cells respond to antigen by differentiating into cells that regulate
activity of the innate and the adaptive immune systems. CD4-positive T cells that
primarily activate other cells are called helper cells and include TH1, TH2, and TH17
subsets. TH1 cells primarily activate pro-inflammatory macrophages and also can
stimulate antibody production by B cells. TH2 cells primarily stimulate antibody
production by B cells. TH17 cells produce IL-17 and recruit neutrophils to combat
infection. T cells that primarily inhibit other cells are referred to as regulatory T cells or
Treg cells.
Inflammation
Acute Inflammation

Acute Inflammation
Acute inflammation results from a local innate immune response that can be induced by
physical injury, surgery, or infection. This inflammation is characterized by the Latin
words calor (heat), dolor (pain), rubor (redness), and tumor (swelling). The innate immune
cells produce cytokines that cause vasodilation and increase vascular permeability. The
resultant fluid accumulation then causes calor, dolor, rubor, and tumor. Inflammation
limits tissue damage by recruiting effector molecules and immune cells that oppose
infection by inducing local blood clotting to physically prevent the infection from
spreading through the bloodstream and by promoting repair of the injured tissue. These
processes typically are regulated by pro-inflammatory and anti-inflammatory
macrophages that were termed M1 and M2 macrophages in 2000 by analogy with TH1
and TH2 lymphocytes.5 Pro- and anti-inflammatory macrophages also are respectively
referred to as classically activated or alternatively activated. Although these classification
systems can be useful for conceptualizing immune responses, they are currently

considered overly simplistic. Substantial plasticity and heterogeneity regulate
macrophage responses to most external stimuli.6
Chronic Inflammation

Chronic Inflammation
Although inflammation typically is self-limiting, chronic inflammation can occur, usually if
the initial infection is not cleared from the site or the inflammatory stimulus is generated
repeatedly. Examples include implant infection, particle-induced osteolysis, chronic
granulomatous disease, inflammatory bowel disease, and chronic allergic inflammation.
Chronic inflammation may lead to substantial damage to the surrounding tissues, which
can occur in patients with osteomyelitis.7
Osteoimmunology
Background

Background
Donald Walker demonstrated that hematopoietic cells of the myeloid lineage are
osteoclast precursors and/or are essential regulators of osteoclast differentiation by the
precursors.8 The studies by Walker were among the first evidence that immune cells
regulate bone homeostasis and turnover and were followed up by elegant lineage
tracing studies directly demonstrating that myeloid lineage cells are the in vivo
osteoclast precursors in rodents and humans.9,10 Regulation of immune lineage cells by
osteoblasts was first hypothesized by Gideon Rodan and Jack Martin in 1981.11 They
proposed that osteoblasts secrete factors that regulate differentiation and activity of
monocytes and osteoclasts (Figure 1). A breakthrough in understanding those
interactions was the demonstration in 1988 that direct cell-to-cell contact with the
osteoblast lineage cells must be present to induce the osteoclast precursors to
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:27 PM
AAOS | Immunology and Inflammation
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001002
5/13

differentiate into mature osteoclasts.12 That finding indicated that the key factor is
expressed on the surface of the osteoblast lineage cells rather than being secreted. A
decade later, two groups of investigators used that information to independently
discover a secreted inhibitor of the cell-surface factor13,14 and, later, the cell-surface
factor itself.15,16 They found that the secreted inhibitor, osteoprotegerin (OPG), is a
decoy receptor member of the TNF receptor superfamily and that the cell-surface factor
is identical to a then newly discovered cytokine of the TNF superfamily that was already
known to be produced by activated T cells and to regulate activity of T cells and dendritic
cells.17,18 Because its receptor, a member of the TNF receptor superfamily, was named
RANK (receptor activator of nuclear factor-?B),17 the cell-surface cytokine is known as
RANK ligand (RANKL). Osteoclast differentiation is tightly controlled by relative changes
in transcription of RANKL and OPG. Therefore, the ratio of the amount of RANKL mRNA
to the amount of OPG mRNA typically is an excellent surrogate measure of osteoclast
differentiation and activity.
Figure 1 Rough sketch depicts the first hypothesis that immune lineage cells are
regulated by osteoblasts (OB). X and Y denote factors secreted by osteoblasts to regulate
differentiation and activity of monocytes and osteoclasts in response to parathyroid
hormone (PTH) or prostaglandin E (PGE). (Adapted with permission from Rodan GA and
Martin TJ: Role of osteoblasts in hormonal control of bone resorption-a hypothesis. Calcif
Tissue Int 1981;33:349-351.)


Definition
Osteoimmunology is an emerging cross-disciplinary field that studies complex regulatory
interactions between immune cells and bone cells. The term osteoimmunology was
coined by Yongwon Choi in 2000 shortly after the discovery of the RANKL-RANK-OPG
system.19 Since that time, knowledge of those reciprocal interactions has become
increasingly complex,20 and the number of studies on this topic continues to grow
exponentially (Figure 2).
Figure 2 Graph shows the number of papers on osteoimmunology listed in PubMed,
which continues to grow exponentially. (Courtesy of Edward M. Greenfield, PhD,
Indianapolis, IN.)

Particle-Induced Osteolysis as an Example of Osteoimmunology
Particle-induced osteolysis that occurs during aseptic loosening of orthopaedic implants
is a classic example of osteoimmunology because it is driven by macrophage-derived
cytokines that induce osteoblast lineage cells to produce RANKL and thereby
substantially increase osteoclast differentiation (Figure 3). Orthopaedic corrosion
products induce a more complex example of osteoimmunology that also involves
lymphocytes and is known by many names, including aseptic lymphocyte-dominated
vasculitis-associated lesions , perivascular lymphocytic infiltration, adverse local tissue
reactions, adverse reactions to metal debris, and trunnionosis.
Figure 3 Illustration shows osteoimmunology of particle-induced osteolysis. IL =

9/3/26, 4:27 PM

interleukin, Mf = macrophage, OPG = osteoprotegerin, RANK = receptor activator of
nuclear factor-?B, RANKL = receptor activator of nuclear factor-?B ligand, TNF = tumor
necrosis factor. (Courtesy of Edward M. Greenfield, PhD, Indianapolis, IN.)
As depicted in Figure 3, polymeric and metallic orthopaedic wear particles substantially
increase production of pro-inflammatory cytokines, such as TNF-a, IL-1a, IL-1ß, and IL-6,
by macrophages.21,22 These responses are thought to require signaling by TLRs;
however, whether the wear particles activate TLRs by inducing release of endogenous
alarmins or whether bacterially derived PAMPs are required is a subject of
controversy.23 IL-1ß and the structurally related IL-18 are transcribed and translated as
immature proteins, known as pro–IL-1ß and pro–IL-18. Pro–IL-1ß and pro–IL-18 are then
proteolytically processed to their active mature forms by large macromolecular
complexes known as inflammasomes. The primary type of inflammasome activated by
orthopaedic wear particles in macrophages is named the NLRP3 inflammasome. NLRP3
is the inflammasome component that transmits particle-induced signals to activate
caspase-1, the protease that processes pro–IL-1ß and pro–IL-18 to mature IL-1ß and IL-
18. The NLRP3 inflammasome is unique in that before activation, a priming signal is
required to increase transcription and translation of pro–IL-1ß and NLRP3 itself. Mature
IL-1ß and IL-18 do not contain typical secretory sequences that target most cytokines for
secretion. In the context of NLRP3 inflammasome activation, IL-1ß and IL-18 are
primarily released through membrane pores formed by a transmembrane protein
known as gasdermin D. Gasdermin D also is initially produced in a pro-form that is
proteolytically processed by caspase-1 before pore formation. A recent study
demonstrated that gasdermin D pores are required for IL-1ß release after macrophage
activation by wear particles in vitro.24
As depicted in Figure 3, the primary role of osteoblasts and other mesenchymal cells
during particle-induced osteolysis is to produce RANKL in response to the macrophage-
derived pro-inflammatory cytokines and, thereby, substantially increase osteoclast
differentiation.21,25 Evidence shows that bone formation by osteoblasts is modestly
reduced during particle-induced osteolysis.26 Although the decreased bone formation is
quantitatively much smaller than the increase in bone resorption, stimulation of bone
formation may counteract the increased resorption and, therefore, remains an attractive
therapeutic approach for particle-induced osteolysis.27

As depicted in Figure 3, a large increase in the number of active osteoclasts from
increased osteoclast differentiation is the primary mechanism responsible for particle-
induced osteolysis.26,28 Therefore, inhibition of bone resorption is an attractive
therapeutic approach.29 In that regard, diphosphonates reduce particle-induced
osteolysis in animal models and blunt the early bone remodeling response after total
joint arthroplasty but have not been effective in patients with ongoing periprosthetic
osteolysis.30 More promisingly, a recent short-term proof-of-concept randomized trial of
the anti-RANKL antibody denosumab reported promising results in patients with
established periprosthetic osteolysis,31 and at least one longer term randomized clinical
trial of denosumab is in progress.32
